hints: Hint 1: Think about what is kept constant in each snapshot. One graph freezes time and looks along the wave, the other watches one point as time passes.
Hint 2: Recall which quantity is a length along the wave and which is a time for one oscillation, so you can match $\lambda$ to distance and $T$ to time.
Hint 3: Remember both vertical axes measure the same thing - how far a particle is from equilibrium - and amplitude is the maximum value of this.
parts.proper_answer: Left graph: y-axis displacement, x-axis distance, $\lambda$ = distance between two adjacent peaks, $A$ = peak height from equilibrium. Right graph: y-axis displacement, x-axis time, $T$ = time between two adjacent peaks, $A$ = peak height from equilibrium.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the two different views**
Think of a progressive wave as a moving snake. You can either take a photograph at one instant and see its shape in space, or you can stare at one single point and watch it move up and down in time. Both views give a sine curve but the horizontal axis is different.

Step 2: **Label the distance graph for wavelength**
For the displacement-distance graph: $$\text{y-axis = displacement, x-axis = distance}$$ Wavelength $\lambda$ is a length, so it belongs here. Mark it as the horizontal distance from one crest to the next crest, or one trough to the next. Amplitude $A$ is the vertical distance from the equilibrium line (0) to the top of a crest.

Step 3: **Label the time graph for period**
For the displacement-time graph: $$\text{y-axis = displacement, x-axis = time}$$ Period $T$ is a time, so it belongs here. Mark it as the horizontal time from one crest to the next crest for that one particle. Amplitude $A$ is marked exactly the same way, from equilibrium to peak.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: The speed of a progressive wave along the string is $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The stationary wave has a period of $40\text{ ms}$.
parts.text:
A horizontal string is stretched between two fixed points $X$ and $Y$. A vibrator is used to oscillate the string and produce a stationary wave. Fig. 4.2 shows the string at one instant in time.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain how the stationary wave is formed on the string.

markscheme_points.text: the incident and reflected waves interfere/superpose
wave (moves along string and) reflects at fixed point/Y/X/end

hints: Hint 1: Start by following the wave made by the vibrator - what happens when it reaches the fixed clamp at X or Y?
Hint 2: Think about what happens when two identical waves travel in opposite directions through each other on the same string.
parts.proper_answer: Progressive wave travels along string and reflects at fixed ends X and Y. Incident and reflected waves of same frequency superpose / interfere to form a stationary wave.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reflection at the fixed ends**
The vibrator sends a progressive wave along the string. When it hits the fixed points X and Y it cannot pass through, so it reflects back. You now have two waves on the same string travelling in opposite directions with the same speed, frequency and wavelength.

Step 2: **Superposition creates the stationary pattern**
Where the two oppositely travelling waves meet they superpose, meaning their displacements add. In most places they interfere constructively and destructively in a fixed pattern, giving fixed nodes of zero amplitude at X and Y and elsewhere, and antinodes of maximum amplitude in between. Because the pattern does not travel, it is a stationary wave.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
A particle on the string oscillates with an amplitude of $13\text{ mm}$. At time $t$, the particle has zero displacement.

Calculate

1. the displacement of the particle at time $(t + 100\text{ ms})$,

2. the total distance moved by the particle from time $t$ to time $(t + 100\text{ ms})$.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the elapsed time of 100 ms with the time for one full oscillation of 40 ms to find how many cycles have passed.
Hint 2: Visualise a particle starting at equilibrium - after a whole number of cycles it returns to the same state, so focus on what the extra half cycle does to displacement.
Hint 3: For total path length, count how many amplitudes are covered in one full back-and-forth cycle, then scale up to 2.5 cycles.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find how many periods fit in 100 ms**
Each particle performs SHM with period $T = 40\text{ ms}$. Number of oscillations: $$N = \frac{100\text{ ms}}{40\text{ ms}} = 2.5$$ So the particle completes two full cycles plus one half cycle.

Step 2: **Displacement after 2.5 cycles**
Displacement is position from equilibrium. Starting at 0, after any whole number of cycles you are back at 0. The extra 0.5 cycle takes you from 0 to max and back to 0 on the opposite side. So: $$\text{displacement at } t+100\text{ ms} = 0\text{ mm}$$ Do not confuse this with distance travelled.

Step 3: **Total distance travelled**
Distance adds up all the path. In one period the particle goes 0 to +A to 0 to -A to 0, which is $4A$. $$\text{distance per period} = 4 \times 13 = 52\text{ mm}$$ $$\text{total distance} = 2.5 \times 52 = 130\text{ mm}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Use the given period of 40 ms to get frequency - remember to convert ms to s first.
Hint 2: Link the progressive wave speed of 30 m s-1 to frequency and wavelength with the wave equation.
Hint 3: Calculate the progressive wavelength from $v$ and $f$ before thinking about the stationary pattern.
Hint 4: Look at Fig. 4.2 and count how many wavelengths fit between the fixed ends X and Y.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Frequency from period**
Frequency is oscillations per second: $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$ $$T = 40\text{ ms} = 40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$ $$f = \frac{1}{40 \times 10^{-3}} = 25\text{ Hz}$$

Step 2: **Wavelength of the progressive wave**
Use the wave equation for the travelling waves that make the pattern: $$v = f\lambda$$ Rearranged: $$\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{30}{25} = 1.2\text{ m}$$ You can also think of it as $\lambda = vT = 30 \times 40 \times 10^{-3} = 1.2\text{ m}$.

Step 3: **Read the stationary pattern length**
Fig. 4.2 shows nodes at X and Y with three half-loops in between. That is 1.5 full wavelengths: $$XY = 1.5\lambda$$ A common slip is to call XY one wavelength. Count nodes: X to first middle node is $\lambda/2$, and so on, giving $3 \times \lambda/2$.

Step 4: **Calculate XY**
$$XY = 1.5 \times 1.2 = 1.8\text{ m}$$
